newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: IATA hits at U.S. over passenger compensation.
newsitem.headline: IATA hits at U.S. over passenger compensation.

text.p: The global airlines body IATA said Friday it was protesting strongly over a U.S. refusal to clear the way for fast compensation for victims of air crashes, accusing Washington of acting "illegally and unwisely."

IATA, the International Air Transport Association which links the world's 232 major carriers, said it had filed a formal objection to the U.S. Department of Transport (DOT) over its proposals on the issue.

And airline industry officials said if the DOT position were allowed to stand, relatives of the dead in the July 17 TWA Boeing explosion off New York could expect to wait months or years before they were compensated for their loss.

A lawyer for 25 families of victims of the disaster, in which 230 people died, filed lawsuits against the constructors and the airline earlier this week, arguing the plane was downed by a malfunction that could have been prevented.

The IATA move was the latest in an effort by the industry to remove long-standing liability limits on compensation as set out in the post-World War II Warsaw Convention which aviation lawyers describe as "grossly inadequate and unsustainable."
The limits currently range from $75,000 in the United States to $150,000 in Europe and $350,000 in Australia.

Many IATA airlines have now signed the two so-called Inter-Carrier Agreements -- the first on liability and the second on implementation -- replacing the limits with a pledge to pay full "compensatory damages."

The agreements, which were filed in July with the DOT in Washington for approval for application in the United States, also relieve the victim or beneficiaries from the need to prove an airline was at fault to receive full compensation.
Earlier this month the DOT said it expected to issue an order by the end of the year that would lift the ceiling.
"No longer will families face the prospect of decades of litigation in an effort to prove the "wilful misconduct' of airlines," the department said in an Oct. 4 statement.
Passengers or their families would be able to recover the full amount of damages without limit, unless the carrier could prove it was not negligent, the statement added.

But IATA, which had wanted the two agreements to go into effect on Nov. 1, said conditions attached by DOT meant that victims of international air crashes and their relatives would still face the $75,000 limit, in some cases for many years, before receiving compensation.

IATA officials said that in its 68-page objection to the proposals filed in Washington Thursday the airline body argues that the DOT terms "are unlawful and unwise" and calls for urgent reconsideration.
It also asserts that the U.S. terms placed harsh restrictions on any legal action.
The officials said the U.S. was seeking to make the company that wrote the ticket responsible for a passenger injured or killed in an air disaster and not the airline on which he was travelling.

"This would undermine the whole principle of inter-lining (writing of tickets by one airline for journeys on one or several other airlines) which is now widespread in the industry," one official declared.
